title: De-escalation and preventing violence
blurb: Spot early warning signs, lead a calm verbal and non-verbal de-escalation and reduce ward triggers, as NICE NG10 sets out.
question: Marcus, 32, detained under section 3, has just been told his section 17 leave is cancelled. He is pacing the corridor, red in the face, shouting and jabbing his finger at two nurses. Other patients are watching. What should the nurse do first?

teach.body: De-escalation is the use of verbal and non-verbal skills, distraction, calming and a change of environment to reduce a person's agitation or anger before it becomes violence. NICE NG10 puts it before every restrictive intervention and says it should continue throughout one. In plain English: notice the storm building early, lower the temperature, and give the person a way to regain control without force.

steps.label: Know the person
steps.sub: Close working relationship; watch mood and composure (1.3.13)

steps.label: Space and calm
steps.sub: Quiet area, not the seclusion room (1.3.14, 1.3.20)

steps.label: PRN per care plan
steps.sub: Individualised, maximum dose and interval set (1.3.10)

steps.label: Restrictive intervention
steps.sub: Last resort if harm is likely; keep de-escalating (1.4.5)

teach.caption: Restrictive interventions are used only when de-escalation and other preventive steps, including PRN, have failed.

head: What you notice
Examples
rows: A sociable person sitting alone and withdrawn
Pacing, clenched fists, tense posture, staring
Recorded in the care plan or advance statement (1.3.16)
teach.caption: Each person's early warning signs and what has calmed them before belong in their care plan (NG10 1.2.10).

rows.label: Stance
values: Squared up, arms folded, close in

rows.label: Eye contact
values: Fixed stare or none at all

teach.caption: NG10 1.3.19: staff regulate their own anxiety and frustration, including posture and eye contact.

root.label: A predictable flashpoint
root.sub: Plan the words before the moment

children.label: Calm request, say what happens next

teach.caption: Leave refused, a failed tribunal or being detained are recognised triggers (NG10 1.2.7).

teach.h: Ward factors that raise or lower risk (NG10 1.2.7)
head: Domain
What helps
rows: Positive, encouraging, emotionally regulated, good leadership
Therapies, exercise, leisure, help with communication
Anticipate detention, leave refused, failed appeals
Unlocked doors where possible, outside space, privacy

teach.h: Scenario: Marcus on the acute ward
teach.body: Staff Nurse Adebayo knows Marcus well, so she becomes the one person who speaks. She stands side-on at a safe distance, keeps her hands open and voice low, and says: 'I can see the news about your leave has really upset you.' A colleague quietly moves other patients away. She offers Marcus the quiet lounge to talk about what happens next with his leave. The flashpoint (a refused request) is recorded in his care plan with what worked.

teach.text: Two classic errors. First, the seclusion room is not a 'calm-down room': NG10 says do not routinely use it for de-escalation because it may feel threatening. Second, if a person holds a weapon, ask them to put it down in a neutral place rather than hand it to you (NG10 1.3.7).

items.label: MDT review of PRN for agitation (1.3.11)
staff carry out a search, 1 same sex (1.3.3)

items: De-escalation comes first and continues during any restrictive intervention.
One staff member leads; others support quietly and move onlookers away.
Calm voice, open stance, safe space, acknowledge feelings, offer choices.
PRN is individualised with a stated maximum dose and interval, never routine on admission.
Use a designated calm area, not the seclusion room; ask for weapons to be put down in a neutral place.

summary: You can now recognise early warning signs of aggression, lead a calm verbal and non-verbal de-escalation and handle known flashpoints. You can also explain how ward factors, PRN planning and care plans reduce the need for restrictive interventions under NICE NG10.

A.q: According to NICE NG10, when a service user becomes agitated, how many staff members should take the primary role in communicating with them?
options: Two, so one can record
One staff member
The whole team present
The most senior person on shift
A.why: NG10 1.3.18: one staff member should take the primary role in communicating, assessing safety and negotiating in a non-confrontational way.

whyNot.0: Two people talking at once can confuse and escalate; one leads while others support.
whyNot.2: A group of staff speaking can feel threatening and increase arousal.
whyNot.3: The lead is the person best placed to communicate, often someone who knows them, not by seniority.

A.q: An agitated patient is holding a broken plate. Following NICE NG10, what should the nurse ask him to do?
options: Hand the plate directly to the nurse
Throw the plate into the bin
Put the plate down in a neutral place
Keep hold of it while they talk
A.why: NG10 1.3.7: ask a service user carrying a weapon to place it in a neutral location rather than hand it over.

whyNot.0: Handing it over brings the weapon towards staff; NG10 advises a neutral location instead.
whyNot.1: Throwing an object is itself an aggressive act and could injure someone.
whyNot.3: Leaving the weapon in his hand keeps the immediate risk in place.

A.q: Which room does NICE NG10 advise against routinely using to help an agitated patient calm down?
options: A comfort room
The garden
The patient's bedroom
The seclusion room
A.why: NG10 1.3.20: in services that use seclusion, do not routinely use the seclusion room to reduce arousal, because the person may perceive it as threatening.

whyNot.0: Comfort rooms are listed in NG10 1.3.14 as places that can aid de-escalation.
whyNot.1: Gardens are among the spaces NG10 suggests for separating agitated service users.
whyNot.2: Bedrooms are listed as possible quiet areas, with staff not left isolated.

B.q: Sofia, 27, is shouting at a nurse about her cancelled visit. Which response best shows verbal de-escalation?
options: 'Shouting won't get you anywhere, so calm down.'
'I can hear how upset you are. Can we sit and sort this?'
'If you carry on, I will have to call for help.'
'Visits are cancelled for everyone today, it's the rules.'
B.why: Acknowledging the feeling and offering a joint way forward communicates respect and empathy (NG10 1.3.17-1.3.18) and invites negotiation.

whyNot.0: Telling someone to calm down dismisses the feeling and is likely to provoke.
whyNot.2: This sounds like a threat; NG10 1.3.12 asks staff to respond to anger in a measured way and avoid provocation.
whyNot.3: Citing a blanket rule closes down negotiation and may be an unjustified restriction.

B.q: A doctor writes 'PRN haloperidol for agitation' for every new admission. What does NICE NG10 say about this practice?
options: It is good practice so medicine is ready if needed
It is acceptable if the nurse decides each dose
PRN should be tailored to the person, not routine
It is acceptable for the first 72 hours of admission
B.why: NG10 1.3.10: do not prescribe PRN routinely or automatically on admission; tailor it, state the rationale, maximum daily dose and interval.

whyNot.0: Routine PRN on admission is exactly what NG10 advises against.
whyNot.1: Nursing judgement does not replace an individualised prescription with stated limits.
whyNot.3: NG10 sets no 72-hour exception for routine PRN prescribing.

B.q: During de-escalation, which non-verbal approach is most appropriate?
options: Stand directly facing the person, close enough to touch
Fold your arms to show you are in control
Keep a steady, fixed stare to show confidence
Stand at an angle, at a safe distance, hands open
B.why: A side-on stance, safe distance and open hands respect personal space and appear non-threatening (NG10 1.3.12, 1.3.19).

whyNot.0: Facing square on and close invades personal space and can feel confrontational.
whyNot.1: Folded arms appear closed and defensive.
whyNot.2: A fixed stare can be read as a challenge.

C.q: Omar, 44, normally chats with staff, but today he is sitting alone, clenching his jaw and muttering after a phone call from his brother. The ward is busy. What is the most appropriate initial action?
options: Increase his observation level to continuous
Approach calmly and ask what is troubling him
Offer PRN lorazepam before he becomes aggressive
Ask security to stand by the lounge door
C.why: NG10 1.3.13 and 1.4.12: sensitively monitor changes in mood and use positive engagement first. A calm approach to explore the trigger (an outside family issue, NG10 1.2.7) is the least restrictive first step.

whyNot.0: Observation is used after positive engagement has failed to reduce the risk (1.4.12).
whyNot.2: PRN is not a first step before he has even been spoken to.
whyNot.3: Visible security escalates and is not a therapeutic first response.

C.q: Ruth, 50, has thrown a chair across the lounge, narrowly missing another patient. Staff have tried talking with her and she declined her PRN. She picks up another chair. Under NICE NG10, what is the position on a restrictive intervention now?
options: It can be used, and de-escalation should continue
It cannot be used until a doctor has seen her
It can be used, and talking with her should stop
It cannot be used because she refused PRN
C.why: NG10 1.4.5: a restrictive intervention may be used when de-escalation and other preventive strategies, including PRN, have failed and there is potential for harm; continue to attempt de-escalation throughout.

whyNot.1: Staff may act in an emergency to prevent harm; a doctor should attend promptly, but harm is not left to happen meanwhile.
whyNot.2: De-escalation continues during the intervention (NG10 1.4.5; COP15 26.66).
whyNot.3: Refusing PRN is part of why preventive steps have failed; it does not bar an intervention.

C.q: After several incidents on a ward, the manager asks what NICE NG10 suggests to reduce violence across the ward. Which measure is most consistent with the guideline?
options: Lock the main door so patients stay on the ward
Cancel group activities to reduce contact
Offer more activities, exercise and outside access
Move all agitated patients into seclusion early
C.why: NG10 1.2.7 lists meaningful activities, physical exercise, easy access to outside space and unlocked doors as ways to reduce violence and restrictive interventions.

whyNot.0: NG10 notes that restricting freedom of movement can itself trigger violence.
whyNot.1: Removing activities increases boredom and frustration, a recognised risk.
whyNot.3: Seclusion is a last-resort restrictive intervention, not a prevention strategy.

reteach.title: Lower the temperature
reteach.question: If you only remembered one idea about de-escalation, what should it be?

blocks.h: One calm voice, space and a way out
blocks.body: De-escalation is about lowering arousal. One person speaks, calmly and respectfully, acknowledging the feeling. Everyone else gives space and moves onlookers away. Offer choices and a quieter place that does not feel like a punishment. Only if harm is likely and these steps, including PRN, have failed is a restrictive intervention used, and even then the talking continues.

steps.label: Space
steps.sub: Quiet area, not the seclusion room

blocks.text: A weapon is put down in a neutral place, not handed to staff.

explain.body: NG10 asks staff to recognise early signs of agitation, irritation, anger and aggression, and to notice changes from a person's usual mood or composure. People are encouraged to name their own triggers, recorded in care plans and advance statements.

test.q: Where should a patient's own triggers and early warning signs of aggression be recorded, according to NICE NG10?
options: In their care plan and advance statement
In the ward's incident log
In the nurse's handover notes
In a letter to their nearest relative
test.why: NG10 1.3.16: include the person's triggers, early warning signs and wishes in care plans and advance statements, and give them a copy.

whyNot.1: Incident logs record events after they occur; they are not a prevention plan.
whyNot.2: Handover notes are temporary and do not involve the patient.
whyNot.3: Sharing with relatives depends on consent and is not where the plan is held.

explain.body: When a person becomes agitated, one staff member takes the primary role: assessing safety, seeking clarification and negotiating in a non-confrontational way. Others stay nearby without crowding and look after other patients.

test.q: What is the role of the lead staff member during de-escalation?
options: To restrain the person if voices are raised
To decide on the patient's PRN dose
To call security as the first step
To assess safety, clarify and negotiate
test.why: NG10 1.3.18: the lead assesses the situation for safety, seeks clarification and negotiates to resolve it non-confrontationally.

whyNot.0: Raised voices alone do not justify restraint; de-escalation comes first.
whyNot.1: PRN doses are set by the prescription, not decided by the lead in the moment.
whyNot.2: Calling security first is escalation, not negotiation.

explain.body: Separate agitated people from others using quiet areas, bedrooms, comfort rooms or gardens, making sure staff are not isolated. A designated calm area helps; the seclusion room should not be routinely used for this.

test.q: A nurse wants to help an agitated patient calm down away from others. Which is the best choice?
options: The seclusion room with the door open
A quiet lounge with colleagues nearby
His bedroom with the nurse alone inside
The ward office behind a closed door
test.why: NG10 1.3.14 and 1.3.20: use quiet areas to aid de-escalation while ensuring staff are not isolated; avoid routine use of the seclusion room.

whyNot.0: Even with the door open, the seclusion room may feel threatening.
whyNot.2: A nurse alone with an agitated person is isolated, which NG10 warns against.
whyNot.3: A closed office isolates the nurse and is not a therapeutic space.

explain.body: Restraint, rapid tranquillisation or seclusion are used only when de-escalation and other preventive strategies, including PRN, have failed and there is potential for harm. They must never punish or humiliate, and de-escalation continues throughout.

test.q: Under NICE NG10, when may a restrictive intervention be used?
options: When a patient refuses a reasonable request from staff
When staff need to show the patient who is in charge
When preventive steps have failed and harm is possible
When the ward is short of staff on a busy shift
test.why: NG10 1.4.5-1.4.6: only if de-escalation and other preventive strategies have failed and there is potential for harm; never to punish or establish dominance.

whyNot.0: Refusal alone is a flashpoint to negotiate, not a ground for restriction.
whyNot.1: Using restriction to establish dominance is prohibited by NG10 1.4.6.
whyNot.3: Staffing shortage is not a lawful or clinical reason to restrict.
